newsitem.title: USA: First Chicago sees 5 pct U.S. holiday sales gain.
newsitem.headline: First Chicago sees 5 pct U.S. holiday sales gain.

text.p: Strong sales of apparel and general merchandise should help retailers post five percent sales gains over 1995 during November and December, according to Diane Swonk, deputy chief economist at First Chicago NBD Corp.

"This is the first time in some time that we've actually seen the more traditional end of the market do better," Swonk told a news conference. General merchandise and apparel sales are expected to rise six percent in November and December, which First Chicago views as the holiday shopping season, compared to a 2.1 percent rise in 1995.
"Part of this strength this year is because last year was so lousy," Swonk said, noting retail bankruptcies before the 1995 holiday season and deep discounting.
But stores will still be offering promotions and financing incentives to lure consumers, which could lead to credit problems down the road, she said.
"We're not really creating money out there, we're just shifting it around in our pockets," she said.
With stores allowing credit for customers who are already stretched on other credit cards, there could be a surge of personal bankruptcies after the holiday season, Swonk said.
Retailers should also see a higher level of consumer charge-offs due to easier credit policies, which make gains in holiday sales even more crucial to retailers, Swonk said.
"They'd better hope to get very good sales in the Christmas season to cushion their balance sheets as spending also slows," she said.
But Swonk also noted that retailers have been more conservative in terms of ordering inventories, which could help prevent some of the deep, deep discounting seen in the past.

One factor helping sales, especially in the Midwest, has been the early cold snap and winter weather, which has helped trigger apparel sales as well as sales of replacement parts for automobiles, Swonk said.
For the Great Lakes Region, she forecast sales up 5.5 percent overall in November and December, compared to a 4.9 percent gain last year.
